name: Eritrean Taita Fit-Fit (Injera Fit-Fit)
region: Eritrean Tigrinya foodways / Horn of Africa
imageAlt: Eritrean taita fit-fit made from torn injera seasoned with berbere and served with green chile
imageCredit: Photo: Temesgen Woldezion, edited by Merhawie Woldezion, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.5.
summary: Eritrean taita fit-fit: torn injera warmed with onion, tomato, tesmi and berbere until the bread absorbs the spicy sauce while retaining some soft, distinct pieces.
lead: Yesterday's injera becomes a fast Eritrean breakfast when it is torn into pieces and folded through fragrant spiced butter, onion, tomato and berbere.
about: Fit-fit is shared across Eritrean and Ethiopian foodways, with names and bread choices varying by language and household. In Tigrinya, injera is commonly called taita, so taita fit-fit refers specifically to the injera-based form rather than kitcha fit-fit made from an unleavened pan bread. The basic structure is torn injera, seasoned fat and berbere; onions, tomato, yogurt, green chile or leftover stew may be added according to the kitchen. This version keeps the dish clearly Eritrean and uses prepared injera so the recipe focuses on the fit-fit technique rather than duplicating a full fermentation project.
story: The dish is a practical example of how Eritrean kitchens reuse bread without treating leftovers as second-rate food. Injera's sourness and porous surface make it especially good at absorbing tesmi and chile seasoning. Wikimedia Commons' long-standing photograph identifies taita fit-fit as a traditional Eritrean food, while Eritrean-focused home-cooking sources document the same torn-bread, berbere and clarified-butter logic. Because closely related fit-fit is also eaten in Ethiopia, this page does not claim an exclusive national origin; it preserves the Eritrean Tigrinya name and preparation context instead.
caveat: Use actual injera for taita fit-fit. A wheat tortilla, pita or ordinary pancake will absorb sauce differently and should not be presented as equivalent. Eritrean tesmi is preferred; plain ghee is a practical substitute but lacks the aromatic seasoning of tesmi. If your berbere is unusually hot, start with half the amount and add more after the bread is coated.
prepNotes: Slightly drier injera absorbs the sauce without collapsing as quickly as very fresh, wet bread.
Pieces about 1 1/2 inches across give a mix of saucy edges and soft centers instead of turning the pan into paste.
Keep the sauce loose before adding bread
Injera absorbs liquid quickly. The onion-tomato base should look glossy and lightly saucy before the bread goes in.
ingredients: 2 large prepared injera or taita, preferably 1 day old, torn into 1 1/2-inch pieces
3 tbsp Eritrean tesmi or niter kibbeh
1 small red onion, finely diced
1 medium ripe tomato, finely diced
1 to 1 1/2 tbsp berbere spice blend, to taste
1/4 cup hot water or light unsalted broth, plus more only if needed
1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
Plain yogurt, optional for serving
1 fresh jalapeño or other mild green chile, sliced, optional for serving
steps: Tear the injera into irregular 1 1/2-inch pieces and spread them on a tray while you prepare the sauce. If the bread feels very wet and fresh, let it air-dry for 10 minutes so the pieces hold their shape better.
Melt the tesmi in a wide skillet over medium heat. Add the onion and cook 5 to 6 minutes, stirring, until translucent with lightly golden edges rather than deeply browned.

Add the tomato and cook 3 to 4 minutes until it softens and releases juice. Stir in the berbere and salt for 20 to 30 seconds, just until the fat turns brick-red and smells strongly aromatic; do not scorch the chile spices.
Pour in 1/4 cup hot water and simmer 1 minute. Checkpoint: the pan should contain a loose, glossy red sauce that coats a spoon but still flows when the skillet is tilted.
Add the torn injera in two batches, folding gently with a broad spatula after each addition so the sauce reaches most surfaces without crushing the bread.

Cook 2 to 3 minutes over medium-low heat. Checkpoint: the injera should be hot all the way through, stained red-orange and soft, but many pieces should remain visibly distinct rather than dissolving into a uniform mash.

If dry patches remain, sprinkle in hot water 1 tablespoon at a time and fold once or twice. If the fit-fit looks soupy, leave it uncovered for 30 to 60 seconds; injera will continue absorbing liquid as it sits.
Taste for salt and berbere, then serve immediately. Offer plain yogurt and sliced green chile separately so diners can adjust richness and heat without changing the base preparation.

name: Tibetan Shapale (Sha Balep)
imageAlt: Tibetan shapale, fried meat-filled pies with crimped edges
imageCredit: Photo: Gaurav Dhwaj Khadka, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
summary: Tibetan shapale, or sha balep: crisp fried wheat pies wrapped around a juicy beef, cabbage, scallion, ginger and garlic filling.
lead: Shapale pairs an unleavened wheat wrapper with a juicy meat-and-vegetable filling, then fries the sealed pies until the outside is blistered and deeply golden.
about: Shapale is also written shapaley, sha phaley or sha balep; the name is commonly glossed as meat bread. Tibetan cook Lobsang Wangdu describes it as a much-loved community food, often appearing at potlucks and served for lunch or dinner with a simple soup. Yak is a traditional meat on the Tibetan Plateau, while beef is a common practical choice in diaspora kitchens. The pies may be circular or half-moon shaped and are fried rather than steamed like momos.
story: Tibetan foodways have always reflected altitude, pastoralism, grain availability and movement between farming and nomadic communities. Smithsonian Folklife material emphasizes barley, dairy and meat as important parts of Tibetan food culture while also documenting dumplings and breads for gatherings and special meals. Shapale belongs to that broader bread-and-meat repertoire, but it should not be reduced to a 'fried momo': the wrapper, filling proportions and frying technique give it its own identity. This home recipe follows Lobsang Wangdu's widely published Tibetan method while scaling it to a manageable batch.
caveat: Ground beef is used here because it is the practical substitute Lobsang Wangdu recommends when yak is not available; it changes the flavor but preserves the meat-pie structure. Keep the filling cold until assembly and seal every edge completely because trapped juices can cause dangerous oil splatter if a pie opens during frying.
prepNotes: Use cold water in the dough
A firm unleavened dough is easier to roll thin and seal around juicy filling than a soft warm-water dough.
Large cabbage or onion pieces can puncture the wrapper and make the seams leak.
Oil around 350°F browns the wrapper while giving the meat enough time to cook through; hotter oil can darken the outside before the center is safe.
ingredients: 4 cups all-purpose flour, plus more for dusting
1 tsp kosher salt
1 1/2 cups cold water, approximately
1 lb 85-90% lean ground beef
1 1/2 cups very finely chopped green cabbage
1 small yellow onion, very finely diced
4 scallions, thinly sliced
1 tbsp finely grated fresh ginger
2 garlic cloves, finely grated
1 1/2 tbsp soy sauce
1 tsp kosher salt for the filling
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
1 tbsp neutral oil for the filling
Neutral frying oil, enough for 1 to 1 1/2 inches in a heavy skillet
steps: Combine flour and salt in a large bowl. Add 1 1/4 cups cold water and mix, adding the remaining water a tablespoon at a time until a firm dough forms. Knead 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and elastic, then cover and rest 30 minutes.

While the dough rests, combine beef, cabbage, onion, scallions, ginger, garlic, soy sauce, filling salt, pepper and 1 tablespoon neutral oil. Mix just until evenly distributed, then refrigerate so the fat stays cool.
Checkpoint: the filling should be moist and cohesive but not watery. If liquid pools in the bowl, drain it before filling so the wrappers can seal.
Divide the dough into 12 equal pieces. Keep unused pieces covered. Roll each into a 6-inch circle about 1/8 inch thick, with the outer rim slightly thinner than the center.

Place about 3 tablespoons filling on one half of each circle, leaving a clean 1/2-inch border. Fold into a half moon, press out trapped air and pinch the edge firmly; crimp or pleat the seam for a second seal.
Heat 1 to 1 1/2 inches frying oil in a heavy skillet to 345-355°F. Lower in 2 or 3 pies at a time without crowding. The oil should bubble steadily around the edges, not smoke or erupt violently.
Fry 3 to 4 minutes per side until deeply golden and blistered. Adjust the burner between batches to keep the oil near 350°F.

Checkpoint: the wrapper should feel crisp and sound hollow when tapped, and the beef filling in the thickest pie must reach 160°F with no pink raw center. If the crust browns before the filling is done, lower the oil temperature for the next batch.
Drain on a rack rather than a flat paper-lined plate so the bottoms stay crisp. Rest 5 minutes before serving because the meat juices inside will be very hot.

name: Cambodian Fish Amok (Amok Trey)
imageAlt: Cambodian fish amok, a steamed coconut fish curry served in a folded banana-leaf container
imageCredit: Photo: Stefan Fussan, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.
summary: Cambodian fish amok, or amok trey: white fish folded into coconut cream and yellow kroeung, then gently steamed with egg until softly set and custard-like.
lead: Fish amok is defined less by raw heat than by perfume and texture: lemongrass, galangal, turmeric and makrut lime season fish that steams in coconut until softly set rather than soupy.
about: Fish amok is one of Cambodia's best-known Khmer dishes. A yellow kroeung paste supplies lemongrass, galangal, turmeric, makrut lime and aromatics; coconut cream and egg create the characteristic soft set around pieces of freshwater or mild white fish. Banana-leaf cups are traditional and gently perfume the mixture, although heatproof ramekins make a practical home alternative. Cambodia's Royal Embassy in London explicitly notes that the original form is wrapped or contained and steamed with egg, which is the method used here.
story: Amok is often promoted as a Cambodian national dish, but its exact historical origin is less certain than tourism shorthand suggests, and steamed curries also exist in neighboring cuisines. What is well documented is the Khmer technique and flavor structure. Kampong Thom's official tourism site describes its local freshwater-fish amok as a coconut, lemongrass, galangal and makrut-lime curry mousse cooked in banana leaf. Keeping the filling gently steamed until just set preserves the texture that separates amok trey from a loose coconut curry.
caveat: Do not replace galangal with ginger and then call the flavor identical; ginger is an emergency substitute but is sharper and less piney. If prahok is unavailable, a small amount of good fish sauce can supply salinity but not the same fermented depth. Ramekins are acceptable for home steaming when banana leaves are unavailable; the cooking vessel changes aroma and presentation more than the core custard texture.
prepNotes: Snakehead and other freshwater fish are traditional choices in Cambodia; cod, catfish, tilapia or another firm white fish are practical depending on where you cook.
Fibrous lemongrass and galangal should become a moist paste, not remain as woody chunks in the custard.
Hard, violent steam can make the egg-coconut mixture puff and weep. Maintain a steady but moderate steam and keep the cups above the water line.
ingredients: 1 1/2 lb firm boneless white fish, cut into 1 1/2-inch pieces
1 stalk lemongrass, tender lower 4 inches only, very thinly sliced
1 1/2 tbsp peeled fresh galangal, finely chopped
1 tbsp chopped fresh turmeric or 1 tsp ground turmeric
4 makrut lime leaves, center ribs removed and leaves finely shredded
3 garlic cloves, chopped
2 small shallots, chopped
1 tsp prahok or Cambodian fermented fish paste, optional but traditional in many versions
1 tbsp fish sauce, plus more to taste
1 tsp palm sugar or light brown sugar
1 1/4 cups full-fat coconut cream, divided
2 large eggs
1 cup baby spinach, young noni leaves if reliably sourced, or thinly sliced napa cabbage for lining
1 fresh red chile, very thinly sliced for garnish
4 banana-leaf cups or 4 heatproof 8-ounce ramekins
Steamed jasmine rice, for serving
steps: If using banana leaves, pass the pieces briefly over a low gas flame or dip them in very hot water until flexible, then fold into leak-resistant cups and secure with toothpicks. Set the cups or ramekins in a steamer before filling so they are easy to move.

Make the yellow kroeung: pound or process lemongrass, galangal, turmeric, 3 makrut lime leaves, garlic and shallots until very finely minced and moist. Add 1 to 2 tablespoons coconut cream if a processor needs help moving the mixture.
Whisk the eggs with 1 cup coconut cream, fish sauce, palm sugar and prahok if using. Stir in the kroeung until the mixture is evenly yellow and fragrant.
Fold in the fish pieces gently. Checkpoint: every piece should be coated in thick coconut-kroeung mixture, with no large dry fibers of lemongrass or galangal visible.
Line each cup with a small handful of greens, then divide the fish mixture among the cups. Do not fill above about three-quarters full because the egg mixture expands slightly as it sets.

Bring 1 to 2 inches water to a simmer in the steamer base. Cover and steam over steady medium heat for 25 to 35 minutes, depending on cup depth. Avoid letting condensation pour directly into the cups if your steamer lid drips heavily.

Checkpoint: the amok should look softly puffed and set around the edges while the center jiggles only slightly when the cup is nudged. A thermometer inserted into the center should read at least 160°F so both fish and egg are fully cooked.
Warm the remaining 1/4 cup coconut cream just until fluid. Spoon a little over each amok and garnish with the remaining finely shredded makrut lime leaf and red chile.
Rest 3 to 5 minutes before serving with jasmine rice. The finished texture should be spoonable and tender, closer to a soft savory custard than to a runny curry sauce.
